fundamentals.title: Sitting & hand position
fundamentals.body: Sit so your elbows are roughly level with the keys, forearms parallel to the floor. Curve your fingers gently like you're holding a small ball — don't play with flat, straight fingers. Wrists stay loose and slightly above the level of the keys, never collapsed below them.

fundamentals.title: Finger numbers (this is how every fingering instruction is written)
fundamentals.body: Both hands use the same numbering: thumb = 1, index = 2, middle = 3, ring = 4, pinky = 5. Right hand thumb (1) sits toward the low/left side of what RH plays; left hand thumb (1) sits toward the high/right side of what LH plays — the thumbs point toward each other in the middle of the keyboard.

fundamentals.title: Finding your way around the keys
fundamentals.body: White keys repeat in a pattern of 7 (A B C D E F G). Black keys come in groups of 2 and 3 — find any group of 2 black keys, and the white key just to its left is C. Middle C is the C nearest the center of the keyboard. Once you can find every C without counting, you can find any note by counting up the musical alphabet from the nearest C.

fundamentals.title: Reading a chord chart (this is your sheet music)
fundamentals.body: You'll never need to read standard notation for this project — chord charts are enough. A bare letter (C, G, D) means a major triad. A letter + 'm' (Cm, Gm) means minor. A letter + '7' (C7, G7) adds a bluesy/tense note. 'maj7' is a soft jazzy color. 'sus4' means suspended — no 3rd, sounds open/unresolved, and almost always resolves back to the plain major right after. A slash chord like 'C/E' means play a C major chord but put E as the lowest (bass) note instead of C — very common in Thai ballads for smooth descending basslines.

chord_shapes.title: Major triad — the shape behind ~half of every chord you'll play
chord_shapes.formula: 1st - 3rd - 5th note of the scale (root, +2 white-key-equivalent steps, +2 more)
chord_shapes.example: C major = C - E - G. G major = G - B - D. F major = F - A - C.
chord_shapes.fingering_lh: 5-3-1 (pinky on root, middle on 3rd, thumb on 5th, reading bottom to top)
chord_shapes.fingering_rh: 1-3-5 (thumb on root, middle on 3rd, pinky on 5th)

chord_shapes.title: Minor triad — same shape, one note moved
chord_shapes.formula: Same as major but the middle note (3rd) drops one half-step (one key, white or black) lower.
chord_shapes.example: C major (C-E-G) becomes C minor (C-Eb-G). A minor is special: it's the ONLY minor chord that uses all-white keys (A-C-E), which is why beginners often start in the key of C/Am.
chord_shapes.feel: Sad, wistful, tense — this is most of the emotional weight in Thai ballads.

chord_shapes.title: 7th chord — adds pull/tension that wants to resolve
chord_shapes.formula: Major triad + one more note, a minor 7th above the root (roughly a whole step below the octave).
chord_shapes.feel: Creates forward motion — almost always leads into the next chord (classic V7 → I motion).
chord_shapes.fingering_lh: 5-3-2-1 or drop the 5th (5-3-1) if your hand is small — the 7th and root matter most

chord_shapes.title: Slash chords — same chord, different bass note
chord_shapes.formula: Chord letter / bass note. Play the full chord with your right hand as normal; your left hand (or your right-hand pinky if playing LH-only) plays ONLY the note after the slash, low.
chord_shapes.example: C/E = C major chord, but E is the lowest note played. Common Thai-ballad move: C → G/B → Am → G, where the bass walks down C-B-A-G step by step under the chords.
chord_shapes.feel: Smooths out the bassline so it doesn't jump around — this is the #1 trick that makes Thai ballad accompaniment sound 'right'.
chord_shapes.fingering_lh: Play just the bass note with your thumb or pinky depending on register; chord goes in RH.

lh_patterns.title: 1. Block chords
lh_patterns.how: Play all notes of the chord together, once per beat (or once per chord change if the song is slow). Left hand alone, or both hands together doubling the chord.
lh_patterns.practice_tip: Get comfortable changing chords smoothly before adding rhythm complexity. This alone is enough to accompany a huge number of slow ballads.

lh_patterns.title: 2. Broken chords (simple)
lh_patterns.when_to_learn: Week 2, once block chords feel automatic.
lh_patterns.how: Instead of all notes at once, play them one at a time, low to high: root, then 3rd, then 5th, repeat. Gives movement without needing a fast tempo.
lh_patterns.practice_tip: Keep the notes perfectly even in timing — a metronome at a slow tempo (60-70 bpm) is your best friend here.

lh_patterns.title: 3. Arpeggio pattern (1-5-3-5)
lh_patterns.how: Left hand plays: root (low), 5th, 3rd, 5th again, in a steady repeating 4-note loop per chord. This is the classic 'rippling' ballad accompaniment sound.
lh_patterns.practice_tip: Practice the pattern on ONE chord (like C) for several minutes until your hand does it without looking, before applying it to a real progression.

lh_patterns.title: 4. Alberti bass
lh_patterns.how: A specific broken-chord order: root, 5th, 3rd, 5th (low-high-middle-high) played evenly, usually a bit faster/lighter than the arpeggio pattern. Very common in classical-leaning pop ballads.
lh_patterns.practice_tip: This is nearly identical in shape to pattern 3 — the difference is mostly in touch (lighter, more even) and tempo (a bit brisker).

lh_patterns.title: 5. Waltz pattern (oom-pah-pah) — for 3/4 time songs
lh_patterns.when_to_learn: Whenever a song in your list is tagged 3/4 — introduce around week 5-6.
lh_patterns.how: Beat 1: low bass note (root) alone. Beats 2 and 3: the rest of the chord (3rd+5th together), lighter. 'OOM-pah-pah, OOM-pah-pah.'
lh_patterns.practice_tip: Exaggerate the accent on beat 1 at first — it's what makes it feel like a waltz instead of just a chord repeated three times.

lh_patterns.title: 6. Thai-ballad rolling arpeggio (with walking bass)
lh_patterns.when_to_learn: Week 5-6, after you're solid on pattern 3 and comfortable with slash chords.
lh_patterns.how: Like pattern 3, but the bass note of each chord follows a stepwise walk-down or walk-up (using slash chords) instead of jumping — e.g. under C, G/B, Am, G the bass plays C-B-A-G in sequence while the rolling arpeggio continues on top.
lh_patterns.practice_tip: This is the single highest-value pattern for this song list — a huge share of the Thai ballads use exactly this move. Worth extra dedicated practice time in week 5-6.

progression_families.name: I - V - vi - IV
progression_families.feel: The single most common pop progression on Earth — upbeat but a little bittersweet. If you learn nothing else, learn this one first.

progression_families.name: vi - IV - I - V
progression_families.feel: The exact same 4 chords as above, just starting from the minor — opens sadder, resolves brighter.

progression_families.name: I - vi - IV - V
progression_families.feel: The classic '50s/doo-wop' loop — warm, nostalgic, very singable.

progression_families.name: vi-centered minor ballad
progression_families.example_in_C: Am - G - F - G  (or similar, centers on the relative minor)
progression_families.feel: Opens and lingers on the sad chord rather than passing through it — typical slow, emotional ballad opener.

progression_families.name: Thai ballad walk-down (slash chords)
progression_families.example_in_C: C - G/B - Am - G  (bass walks C-B-A-G)
progression_families.feel: THE signature sound of Thai pop ballads. Pairs with the rolling-arpeggio pattern (#6 above). Learning this progression + pattern combo unlocks the largest single cluster of songs in your list.

progression_families.name: I - IV - V (three-chord basic)
progression_families.example_in_C: C - F - G  (sometimes C - F - C - G)
progression_families.feel: The simplest possible progression — folk, country, blues-adjacent. Great confidence-builder.

progression_families.name: ii - V - I
progression_families.feel: A little jazzier/smoother resolution, common inside verses of more sophisticated pop songs.

progression_families.name: 12-bar blues form
progression_families.example_in_C: C-C-C-C / F-F-C-C / G-F-C-C (4 bars each of I, then IV, then a I-V-IV-I turnaround)

progression_families.name: Complex / other
progression_families.example_in_C: Varies — modulations, jazz chords, non-diatonic movement
progression_families.feel: Save these for late in the 2 months, or treat as long-term Reference-tier songs.

melody_technique.title: Why by ear, not sheet music
melody_technique.body: There's no melody transcription in this app — partly because a song's melody (unlike chord symbols) is the copyrighted part of a song, so it can't be reproduced here, and partly because ear-training is the more useful skill long-term: once you can find a melody by ear over a chord you already know, you can do it for ANY song, not just the ones someone transcribed for you.

melody_technique.title: Finding the melody note by ear
melody_technique.body: Play the chord for that moment in the song with your left hand, then hum or sing the melody note against it while it rings. Most melody notes are one of the chord tones (root/3rd/5th) or a note one step away from one — try each chord tone against your hum until one matches, then try the note just above or below it. This gets fast with practice; it's a skill, not a lookup.

melody_technique.title: Combining melody (RH) with your LH pattern
melody_technique.body: Don't try to add a fully harmonized right hand — start with just the single melody note, played on the beat, while your left hand keeps whatever accompaniment pattern you already know for that song. Once that's solid, you can thicken the melody note with an octave or a third below it for a fuller sound.

melody_technique.title: Octave placement and simple phrasing
melody_technique.body: Play the melody an octave (or two) above where your left hand sits, so the two hands don't collide. Hold long notes for their full length rather than clipping them, and take a tiny breath/lift at the same places a singer would breathe — that's most of what makes a melody sound musical rather than mechanical.

melody_technique.title: A simple daily drill
melody_technique.body: Pick one short phrase (4-8 notes) from a song you already know the chords to. Loop that phrase on the recording, hum it until it's automatic, then find it on the keyboard one note at a time. Once you have it, play it 5 times in a row cleanly before moving to the next phrase — same 'clean reps' rule as the Deliberate Practice method.

practice_method.title: How to learn any new song in ~20 minutes once you know its pattern
steps: 1. Look up the song's key and progression family in the hub. If you already know that family, skip straight to step 3.
2. If it's a new family: practice just the chord changes, hands separate, slowly, with no rhythm pattern yet — just clean changes.
3. Add the LH pattern tagged for this song. Practice it on ONE chord first, then move through the full progression slowly (60-70 bpm).
4. Add your right hand — easiest is just singing the melody yourself while LH accompanies. Optionally RH doubles the chord tones softly.
5. Gradually increase tempo toward the song's real speed over a few practice sessions — don't jump to full speed immediately.
6. Play through with the chart in front of you (you are NOT required to memorize) while following the recording/video for timing.
